skills.name: visionos-headset-build
skills.description: Use this when building a visionOS app on a connected Mac and pairing, installing, and launching it on a physical Apple Vision Pro.
skills.content:
---
name: visionos-headset-build
description: >-
  Use this when building a visionOS app on a connected Mac and pairing,
  installing, and launching it on a physical Apple Vision Pro.
---
# Build a visionOS app and run it on a Vision Pro

## Project
1. Work on the connected Mac (machine-targeted Shell), never the Linux box. Confirm `xcodebuild -showsdks` lists `xros` and `xrsimulator`, and find an Apple Vision Pro simulator UDID with `xcrun simctl list devices available`.
2. Generate the project with XcodeGen (`project.yml`) or have Claude Code on the Mac create it; pure SwiftUI + RealityKit. Find the signing team from an existing project (`grep DEVELOPMENT_TEAM`) or `security find-identity -v -p codesigning`, and use automatic signing.
3. Add launch arguments (e.g. `-openVolume`, `-openImmersive`, `-detailBot <id>`) that open each 3D scene on launch, so simulator screenshots need no taps. Capture with `xcrun simctl io <udid> screenshot`, copy to the box, and look at every image before sending it.
4. For extruded/beveled 3D characters, place face details (eyes) from the mesh's measured front face (`visualBounds`), not from the base extrusion depth, or they end up buried inside the body. Use unlit materials so they read in any lighting.

## Pairing the headset
1. On the headset: Settings > General > Remote Devices, and keep that screen open. Mac and headset on the same network.
2. Confirm it's broadcasting: `dns-sd -B _remotepairing-manual-pairing._tcp local.` (kill after a few seconds).
3. Run the pair command in a persistent session so it survives between shell calls: `screen -dmS pair sh -c 'script -q pair.log xcrun devicectl manage pair --device "<headset name>" --timeout 600'`. A code then appears on the headset; ask the user for it.
4. Submit the code with a carriage return in one go: `screen -S pair -p 0 -X stuff $'<code>\r'`. Check `pair.log` for "Paired with device".
5. After any failed attempt the headset refuses new ones ("closed by remote side"); have the user back out of Remote Devices and reopen it, then start a fresh pair. Codes from cancelled attempts never work.

## Install and launch
1. Developer Mode must be on (headset Settings > Privacy & Security > Developer Mode, restart, confirm). Check with `xcrun devicectl device info details --device <udid> | grep -i 'developer mode'`. "Does not support tunnel connections" usually means it's off.
2. Build for device with `-destination 'platform=visionOS,id=<udid>' -allowProvisioningUpdates`.
3. `xcrun devicectl device install app --device <udid> <path>/Debug-xros/<App>.app`.
4. Launch with a timeout so a sleeping headset can't hang the job: `perl -e 'alarm 45; exec @ARGV' xcrun devicectl device process launch --terminate-existing --device <udid> <bundle id>`. If it times out, the install still counts; tell the user to open the app from the home view.
5. Keep the Mac awake for long builds with `caffeinate -dims` and kill only the PID you started.

name: mac-native-grok-dev
description: >-
  Use this when doing iOS, macOS, visionOS, Swift, Expo, or Xcode work through
  Grok Bot on a connected Mac.
---
# Mac native development on a connected Mac

## Goal
Run Apple toolchain work (Xcode, simulators, Swift, CocoaPods/SPM, local builds) on the user's registered Mac, never on the Linux box.

## Steps
1. Call `ListMachines` and pick a connected Mac. Pass that `machineId` to Shell, Read, CopyToBox, and CopyFromBox for every Mac-side action.
2. Tell the user the next commands run on their Mac. Machine-targeted tools need approval, so batch related commands.
3. Verify the toolchain before a big build: `xcodebuild -showsdks`, `xcrun simctl list devices available`, `swift --version`.
4. Keep product repos and DerivedData on the Mac filesystem.
5. Prefer `xcrun simctl` for Simulator boot, install, launch, screenshot, openurl; `xcodebuild -scheme ... -destination ...` for native builds; for taps, gestures, typing, permissions, or a live preview stream, use serve-sim.
6. For screenshots or artifacts the chat needs, write under an allowed Mac path (e.g. Documents), then CopyToBox and attach from the box.
7. Use a cloud agent for remote-friendly repo work; use the Mac when the task depends on Simulator, signing, or local Xcode.
8. For long builds, keep the Mac awake with caffeinate.

## Do not
- Run xcodebuild, simctl, or Swift compiles on the Linux box
- Assume every Mac path is readable by CopyToBox (avoid /tmp; prefer home/Documents)
- Start a second long Mac job without checking the first is still healthy

skills.name: mac-caffeinate
skills.description: Use this when long Mac builds, tests, or simulator work might let the machine sleep and kill the session.
skills.content:
---
name: mac-caffeinate
description: >-
  Use this when long Mac builds, tests, or simulator work might let the machine
  sleep and kill the session.
---
# Keep the Mac awake with caffeinate

Prevent idle sleep from interrupting builds, tests, or Simulator work. Tell the user when caffeinate starts and stops.

Flags: `-i` idle sleep, `-d` display sleep, `-m` disk sleep, `-s` system sleep on AC, `-u` assert user activity, `-t <seconds>` timeout, `-w <pid>` hold until a process exits. Typical for builds: `-dims`.

Patterns:
1. Wrap one command: `caffeinate -dims xcodebuild ...`
2. Tie to a PID: `caffeinate -dims -w <build_pid>`
3. Multi-step session: start `caffeinate -dims` in the background, note its PID, and kill only that PID when the work ends.

Always clean up; never leave a forever caffeinate running, and don't kill caffeinate processes you didn't start.

skills.description: Use this when controlling or streaming an Apple Simulator with npx serve-sim (taps, gestures, buttons, camera, permissions, AX) beyond basic simctl.
skills.content:
---
name: serve-sim
description: >-
  Use this when controlling or streaming an Apple Simulator with npx serve-sim
  (taps, gestures, buttons, camera, permissions, AX) beyond basic simctl.
---
# Drive Apple Simulator with serve-sim

Use `npx serve-sim` on the connected Mac for richer Simulator control than simctl: taps, gestures, hardware buttons, typing, rotation, permissions, camera injection, accessibility tree, CoreAnimation debug, and a live preview stream.

Prereqs on the Mac: macOS, Xcode CLT, Node 18+, a booted simulator (`xcrun simctl list devices booted`).

Start/stop: `npx serve-sim --detach -q` (JSON with pid, port, url, streamUrl), `npx serve-sim --list -q`, `npx serve-sim --kill`. Default preview :3200, stream :3100. Always kill when done.

Coordinates are normalized 0..1. Commands: `tap <x> <y>` (use for taps), `gesture '<json>'` for multi-step drags on one socket, `button home|swipe_home|app_switcher|lock|siri|side_button`, `type "text"`, `rotate ...`, `permissions grant|revoke|reset|list <perm> <bundle-id>`, `camera <bundle-id> --file path`, `ui appearance dark`, accessibility tree at `curl -s http://localhost:3100/ax`.

Gotcha: each `gesture` call opens its own WebSocket, so splitting begin/end looks like a long-press. Prefer the AX tree over guessing coordinates. Don't bind to 0.0.0.0 on untrusted networks.

---
name: vision-pro-bot-getting-started
description: >-
  Use this as the imported Vision Pro Bot's first conversation with its new
  owner, to set up their Mac, headset, and project.
---
# Getting started

I build Apple Vision Pro apps in pure SwiftUI and RealityKit on your Mac, verify them in the visionOS simulator, install them on your headset, and send you screenshots as I go.

Ask these one at a time, waiting for each answer:
1. What should I call you, and what would you like to build first? (An app idea, an existing repo to port, or a concept demo.)
2. Which Mac should I build on? Make sure the Grok Bot desktop app is open there so I can run commands on it, then I'll check Xcode and the visionOS SDK.
3. Do you have a Vision Pro you want to install on? If yes, I'll walk you through pairing it with that Mac and turning on Developer Mode.
4. Is there a GitHub repo with assets or code I should start from? If so, connect GitHub (or confirm it's connected) and tell me the repo.
5. Where should new projects live on your Mac? (Default: ~/Documents/GitHub.) Should I commit locally only, or also push to a repo?

Then:
- Save the answers as memories (name, Mac, headset name, project folder, git preference).
- Check the toolchain on the Mac (`xcodebuild -showsdks`, visionOS simulators).
- Start the first build using the visionos-headset-build skill, and send a first simulator screenshot as soon as there is one.
